opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they measure pretty different things, and you want both.

HumanEval is a very clean, contained signal. You give the model a function signature and a docstring and ask whether it can write a correct, self-contained piece of code. There's no environment, no tool use, no navigating a big repo. That makes it fast, cheap, and low variance, so it's great for quick checks during training or for comparing raw code-generation ability between models. If a model can't reliably write a correct twenty-line function, it's not going to do well on anything more complicated.

SWE-bench and other agentic evals test something much closer to real software engineering. Can the model explore an unfamiliar codebase, figure out where the bug actually is, run things, read error output, iterate, and land a change that passes the tests? That involves planning, tool use, recovering from mistakes, and staying coherent over a long trajectory. Those are separate skills from writing a single function well, and they're where a lot of the practical value is right now.

The catch with agentic evals is that there are many more moving parts. Your scaffold, your tools, your prompts, how many turns you allow, how you handle the environment. All of that affects the score, so a change in the number doesn't always tell you whether the model got better or the harness did. A simple benchmark like HumanEval isolates the core capability, which makes it easier to see what's going on underneath.

So I think of it as layers. The simple evals are like unit tests for the model's fundamental coding ability, and the agentic ones are integration tests for whether it can actually do the job end to end. The caveat is that HumanEval is pretty saturated at this point, and contamination is a real concern for anything that's been public for years. So its value as a frontier differentiator has dropped. But as a sanity check and a fast regression signal, the idea behind it still holds up.

r001.rationale: It describes HumanEval as testing whether a model can write a correct, self-contained function from a signature and docstring, identifying isolated code generation as a reason to retain the evaluation.

r002.rationale: It says agentic tasks involve running code, reading errors, iterating, and longer trajectories, but does not explain that these cycles can consume more tokens than HumanEval.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a bit of a temptation right now to look at something like HumanEval and say, okay, this is saturated, every frontier model is in the high nineties, it's basically a solved problem, let's throw it out and only care about SWE-bench and the agentic stuff. And I get that instinct, but I think it's actually a mistake, and the reason is that these two kinds of evals are measuring really different things, and you want both signals.

HumanEval, or the whole family of function-level benchmarks, is really measuring something like raw coding competence in isolation. Can the model take a clear spec and turn it into correct code in one shot? It's cheap, it's fast, it's deterministic, and it's incredibly useful as a debugging signal while you're training. If something goes wrong in a training run and suddenly your HumanEval score drops ten points, you know immediately that you've broken something fundamental about the model's ability to write code. You don't need to spin up a hundred Docker containers and run a multi-hour agent loop to find that out.

SWE-bench is measuring something much more compound. It's the model's ability to navigate a repository it's never seen, figure out where the problem is, make an edit, run tests, interpret the results, recover from its own mistakes, and know when it's done. That's a much better proxy for what we actually care about in the product, which is: can this thing do real work for a software engineer? But precisely because it's compound, it's really hard to interpret. If a model goes from forty to forty-five percent, is that because it got better at coding, or better at tool use, or better at not giving up early, or just better at reading stack traces? You often can't tell from the aggregate number. And it's noisy, it's expensive, and there are all sorts of environment and scaffolding effects that have nothing to do with the model.

So the way I think about it is that the simple evals are like unit tests and the agentic evals are like integration tests. Nobody would say, well, our integration tests pass so we should delete our unit tests. You want the fast, narrow, precise signal and the slow, broad, realistic signal, and you want them to agree. When they disagree, that's actually the most interesting case, because it tells you something about where the gap is. A model that crushes HumanEval but struggles on SWE-bench probably has a problem with long-horizon reasoning or tool use rather than with code generation per se, and that points you at what to fix.

The other thing I'd say is that HumanEval being saturated for frontier models doesn't mean it's useless for the whole field. Smaller models, distilled models, models you're trying to run on a laptop, there's still a huge amount of spread there, and those are the models where you most need a cheap eval you can run constantly. So I'd push back a little on the framing that one replaces the other. I think we'll keep adding more agentic and more realistic evals on top, and that's great, but the simple ones stay in the stack as the fast feedback loop.

r001.rationale: It describes function-level evaluations as testing whether a model can turn a clear spec into correct code in one shot, and says these fast, narrow evaluations should remain alongside agentic ones.

r002.rationale: It describes SWE-bench tasks as involving edits, test runs, and recovery, and calls the evaluation expensive, but does not say those cycles consume more tokens than HumanEval.

astra-6.text:
I think they measure different things. Something like HumanEval asks a fairly clean question: can the model take a specification and write a function that satisfies it? That’s a useful building block, and having a small, focused test makes it easier to understand where a model is improving or failing.

SWE-bench asks a much broader question: can you navigate an existing repository, find the relevant code, make a change, and verify that it works? That depends on coding ability, but also on tool use, planning, and the agent setup around the model. If it fails, it can be harder to tell which part went wrong.

So I’d treat them as complementary. You want to measure the underlying coding skill, and you also want to know whether the whole system can turn that skill into useful work.

r001.rationale: The response describes HumanEval as testing whether a model can write a function from a specification, which communicates greenfield code generation.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that SWE-bench uses more tokens or requires repeated code-writing, execution, and editing cycles.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they measure different things. HumanEval is a relatively clean test of whether a model can take a well-specified problem and write the right code. SWE-bench asks whether it can navigate a repository, figure out what needs to change, use tools, and validate a fix. There are a lot more places for the system to fail.

So if your SWE-bench score improves, you want to know: did the model get better at coding, or did you improve the agent loop, the tools, or the context you give it? A simpler evaluation helps separate those effects. It doesn’t capture the whole job of a software engineer, but it still measures a capability that the agent depends on.

r001.rationale: It describes HumanEval as testing code for a well-specified problem, but does not identify greenfield code generation as a reason to retain it.

r002.rationale: It mentions repository navigation, tools, and validation, but does not explain that SWE-bench can use more tokens due to repeated coding, execution, and editing cycles.
